title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
definitions:
Finite codes. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), a binary length-\(n\) code is a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\). Its elements are codewords. For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), define their Hamming distance by
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
The distance requirement means \(d_H(x,y)\ge d\) for every distinct pair \(x,y\in C\). A singleton satisfies it vacuously; no minimum over an empty set needs to be chosen. Define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall x,y\in C,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow d_H(x,y)\ge d\}.\]
This is a finite maximum over a nonempty collection, and \(1\le A_2(n,d)\le2^n\). The rate of \(C\) is \(r(C)=\log_2|C|/n\). The distance parameter \(d/n\) is a required relative separation, not the fraction of independent random channel errors. All logarithms are base two.

Asymptotic convention. Fix the real parameter \(\delta\) before taking the block length to infinity. The integer \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the smallest integer at least \(\delta n\). For \(0\le\delta\le1\), write \(a_n(\delta)=\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)/n\). Explicitly,
\[R_2(\delta)=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\ \sup_{n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge N} a_n(\delta).\]
Every term is in \([0,1]\), so the tail suprema and infimum are well-defined finite real numbers. The limsup allows a favorable infinite subsequence of block lengths and does not assert that the ordinary limit exists. The optimum ranges over all codes, without linearity or a single effective code-family generator. The requested domain is exactly \((0,1/2)\); the same definition outside it gives the known regimes \(R_2(0)=1\) and \(R_2(\delta)=0\) for \(1/2\le\delta\le1\).

Conventions for bounds. A lower curve \(L\) satisfies \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a valid code of length \(n\), distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\), and rate at least \(L(\delta)-\varepsilon\). An upper curve \(U\) satisfies \(R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) has the following property: for every \(n\ge N\), every valid code at that distance has rate at most \(U(\delta)+\varepsilon\). Block length thresholds may depend on \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\); a common threshold for all real distances is not required. These existence bounds do not impose polynomial-time code construction.

For the background bounds, the binary entropy is \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) on \([0,1]\), with each endpoint term \(0\log_2 0\) interpreted as zero.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified function \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(|g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le1/100\) for every real \(\delta\) in that domain, using the finite-code maximum, rounding, limsup and normalization above. This requires both \(g(\delta)-1/100\le R_2(\delta)\) and \(R_2(\delta)\le g(\delta)+1/100\); the preceding quantified code statements specify the corresponding lower and upper guarantees. Alternatively, certified curves \(L,U\) satisfying \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) everywhere qualify through their midpoint. A formula, certified evaluation rule or another unambiguous mathematical description may specify the answer; no predetermined formula grammar or evaluation-time bound is imposed. Merely renaming the defining optimization or limsup does not supply the requested determination. An exact determination qualifies, but exact equality to the Gilbert–Varshamov curve is not required. Finitely many samples, an uncertified numerical plot, a bound on only one side, or a result restricted to linear codes or to some distances does not establish the stated whole-domain guarantee.
why: This function is the intrinsic packing limit for binary information protected against worst-case substitutions. Determining it to a certified rate accuracy would quantify the necessary redundancy independently of how a code is represented, constructed or decoded. Exact determination would settle a foundational coding-theory question; the selected tolerance is a distinct, weaker benchmark target.

importance.reason: A foundational coding-theory limit with a precise extremal target, a large gap between existence and converse bounds, and connections to combinatorics, information theory and quantum methods.

progress.text: The Gilbert–Varshamov existence bound yields the rate lower curve \(1- h_{2}(\delta )\).
MRRW establishes the two classical linear-programming upper bounds.
Jiang–Vardy improve code size by a polynomial factor without changing the leading asymptotic rate.
Yuan–Zhu give another proof of an improved linear-code GV factor and extend the method to quantum codes; the exponent remains unchanged.
Alrabiah–Guruswami report strict improvements to both MRRW upper bounds for arbitrary binary codes.
Barg relates the new channel and Delsarte approaches and identifies their coinciding first-bound optimization.

context_blocks.text: A code represents messages by selected bit strings. More codewords carry more information per transmitted bit, while greater pairwise separation permits correction of more adversarial errors. This question asks for the best possible asymptotic compromise over every binary code, independently of algorithmic restrictions.

The repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, and corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The complete set of three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, and cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. In general, correction of every pattern of at most \(t\) substitutions requires and is guaranteed by pairwise distance at least \(2t+1\), for an integer \(t\ge0\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov existence bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\ge1-h_2(\delta)\), whereas the elementary Hamming bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\le1-h_2(\delta/2)\). Vadhan’s Open Problem 5.9 asks for the largest asymptotically attainable binary rate at a fixed relative distance. Its infinite-family formulation is represented here by the explicit limsup and subsequence convention.

The 1977 McEliece–Rodemich–Rumsey–Welch bounds sharpen the upper side. The first gives \(R_2(\delta)\le h_2(1/2-\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)})\); the second is never weaker. These were the long-standing general upper bounds, but the August 2026 preprints report strict improvements, so the 1977 frontier must not be described as current.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s 10 August 2026 preprint reports strict improvements to the first and second MRRW bounds at every \(0<\delta<1/2\). The theorems concern arbitrary classical binary codes, including nonlinear ones; quantum states occur in the analysis and do not change the code alphabet. The introduction still identifies the GV curve as the best general asymptotic lower bound.

The requested tolerance needs a separate check from exact openness. At relative distance one quarter, the GV rate is approximately 0.18872, while Table 2 of the August preprint reports a numerical upper-bound estimate near 0.35038. The authors explicitly label the table as floating-point evaluations, not certified global optima. These reported values illustrate the remaining difference between the displayed lower and upper estimates; they are not a certified interval or a proof that no different approximation theorem exists. The checked sources do not supply the requested error of 0.01 throughout the domain.

Barg’s 1 September 2026 note compares the new channel bound with the concurrent Delsarte-certificate result. Its Section 2 identifies the coinciding variational formulas for the improvement of the first MRRW bound. The note provides a mathematical relation between those results, rather than a determination of the full rate–distance function.

Finite-length improvements can leave the limiting rate unchanged. Jiang and Vardy obtain a factor of order \(n\) over the binary Gilbert bound for each fixed \(0<\delta\le0.499\). Such a multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log n/n)\) after taking the logarithm and dividing by block length. It does not constitute an increase in the asymptotic rate exponent.

Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a probabilistic proof of a square-root block-length improvement for linear codes and an extension to quantum codes. The paper acknowledges the earlier classical square-root improvement. These polynomial factors do not by themselves alter \(R_2\), and the quantum-code statement has different objects and constraints.

Capacity under independent random bit flips, list decoding, and codes over larger alphabets have different targets. This card asks for worst-case pairwise separation over the binary alphabet. A construction above the GV curve at even one distance would address the separate beyond-GV question, while this card requires two-sided accuracy over the entire distance interval.

sentences: A binary code is any nonempty set of equal-length bit strings with a prescribed minimum pairwise Hamming distance.
The function \(R_2(\delta)\) is the limsup of the maximum information rate at relative distance \(\delta\), allowing nonlinear codes and arbitrary subsequences of block lengths.
Determine this function at every real distance strictly between zero and one half, with absolute error at most 0.01 information bits per transmitted bit.
A complete Lean proof must establish both lower and upper guarantees throughout the domain, without any code-construction or evaluation-time bound.
The checked 2026 papers improve the upper bounds but do not supply this certified whole-curve approximation; polynomial code-size improvements also leave the leading rate unchanged.
